items.title: Acting on foreign widgets needs a consent boundary automation cannot reach
items.body:
Once a mind can act on a widget tree the OS did not write, the permission model has to grade consequences, not verbs. The failing sequence, spelled out by GPT-6 Astra red-teaming the design:

> The agent is permitted to fill a form. It then `invoke`s an accessible button labelled "Allow" in another window. The broker sees a permitted verb; the action authorises credential access or a purchase.

Requirements, before any foreign-app `act` ships:

- **The broker derives authority** from the caller's identity, the grant's scope and the target's identity. A grade the caller declares is not evidence.
- **Read, text-entry, activation and submission are separate permissions.** An unknown foreign action is unknown impact, not "probably safe".
- **The desktop's own consent UI is outside automation authority.** Consent must arrive through a trusted input path; an accessible label cannot authenticate it. Otherwise the approval work in #27 can be answered by the thing asking for approval.
- **Grants bind to an application instance and expire**; handles are revalidated immediately before dispatch, because trees change underneath you.
- **Accessible text is untrusted content**, never instructions, and may hold secrets even outside password fields.
- Same-UID processes are not a boundary: an agent that can reach the raw accessibility bus bypasses the broker entirely. Decide whether that is acceptable on a single-user machine and write down the answer.

Related: #27 (approvals bound to a run and the OS's grades), #40 (the a11y client), #39 (the switch).

Size: design first, then days. Nothing in #40's act path should land before this is settled.

items.title: infra: native systemd wheeld as the default production deployment
items.body:
Makes the **native systemd path the default production deployment**, with Docker demoted to a
documented, supported alternative. Proposal: `docs/proposals/wheeld-native-production.md`.

Operator directive: *"i'd rather use that than docker"*, then *"you can use docker for this
instance but going forward i'd like the default to be wheeld."* So the live box stays on Docker;
the migration here is a rehearsed procedure, not something anyone runs this week.

**No `crates/` changes.** Every property is earned with systemd, shell, and the binary's existing
behaviour. Where a real fix needs Rust it is written down as a follow-up with an owner (F1–F6),
not reached for here.

## The crux: guarantees compose and Caddy used to earn

| Guarantee | Was | Now | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nothing published to the network | compose `ports: 127.0.0.1:` | binary default + `--bind ${BIND_ADDR}` + `ExecStartPre` refusal + **`ExecStartPost` measures the real socket with `ss`** | **stronger** — and `ufw` is now authoritative, with no Docker iptables rules nobody wrote |
| The signup gate runs before the board | `depends_on: service_completed_successfully` | `wheel-signup-gate.service`, which `wheel-web` `Requires=`/`After=` | **equal, and fixes a real regression** — it used to be shell inside `install.sh`, so it ran once at install and a reboot brought the board up unchecked |
| Signup closed, operator-token bootstrap | wheeld + compose | wheeld + the gate unit | equal |
| Body limits, HSTS, XFF overwrite | Caddy | same Caddy, same Caddyfile | equal |
| A ceiling on a runaway agent | **nothing** (compose sets no `mem_limit`/`pids_limit`/`cpus`) | §5 limits | stronger |
| Honest client attribution behind the proxy | one container IP an agent couldn't send from | `127.0.0.1` = every local process, agents included | **WEAKER — cannot be reproduced.** Stated plainly; tunnel mode (the default) sets no trusted proxy at all, so it's TLS-mode only. Follow-up F2 |

## Hardening: deliberate, not maximal

Every agent runs inside `wheeld.service`'s cgroup, so each directive constrains the code Wheel
exists to run. **Rejected with measurements**: `SystemCallFilter=` (breaks `unshare -Urm` + mount —
bwrap/Chromium), `RestrictNamespaces=` (breaks `unshare` outright), `ProcSubset=pid` (hides
`/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/cpuinfo`), `LimitNPROC=` (counts per uid, not per cgroup). Added:
`ProtectProc=invisible`, `ProtectClock/Hostname/KernelLogs`, `RestrictRealtime`, empty
`CapabilityBoundingSet=`, `PrivateDevices`, `LimitCORE=0` (a core dump of wheeld contains
`master.key`).

**Measurement changed the design three times**, which is the argument for the probe existing:

- The `AF_NETLINK` row would have shipped with a **false** justification. Dropping it does *not*
  break DNS (glibc falls back). It breaks `ss` — which `wheeld-ready` uses to prove the loopback
  bind, so dropping it would make the strongest guarantee above unverifiable.
- The `SystemCallFilter` rejection rested on a wrong claim about `unshare`: plain `unshare`
  survives the filter; only the `mount` after it fails.
- `ProtectSystem`/`ProtectHome` were briefly "verified" by a probe that was really observing
  ordinary file permissions (`wheel` can't write `/usr/local` or read `/root` either way). The
  mutation harness caught it by removing both directives and watching nothing turn red.
- A fourth correction is in the diff's history: I claimed `CapabilityBoundingSet=` breaks `ping`.
  It doesn't — `ProtectSystem=strict` makes `/usr` `nosuid` so the file capability is ignored
  rather than fatal, and Ubuntu's `ping_group_range` default needs no capability. The container
  also can't measure the real cost (`ip_unprivileged_port_start=0`), so the probe now asserts only
  what it can honestly observe.

## Limits that fail towards the agent

**`OOMPolicy=continue` is the one line everything else depends on.** systemd's default is `stop`:
without it, one agent hitting `MemoryMax` makes systemd stop `wheeld` and every other project's
agents. Measured, both directions — with the default the unit ends `failed`/`Result=oom-kill` and
the parent dies; with `continue` the child is killed and the parent stays `active`.

`MemoryMax=2.8G` protects *the box* (sshd survives), not wheeld — the kernel picks by RSS, usually
the agent but not guaranteed; residual stated, F3 is the fix. Plus `MemoryHigh`, `MemorySwapMax`,
`TasksMax=4096`, `LimitNOFILE=65536`, `CPUQuota=150%`, all in an overridable drop-in.

## Install, upgrade, rollback — and not colliding with `sdk/auto-update`

This lane owns the **operator-initiated** lifecycle; `sdk/auto-update` owns the daemon-initiated
one. Three rules, each a change: never delete `*.prev`; use the same swap shape (`.new` →
hard-link `.prev` → `rename(2)`); refuse to move the box backwards without `--allow-downgrade`.
**Rule 2 is a bug fix** — `install.sh` previously `mv -f`'d over the top and kept no `.prev`, so an
operator upgrade destroyed the daemon's rollback point. A failed upgrade now restores the previous
generation automatically and exits non-zero, and `--rollback` goes back on demand without a build.

## Toolchain, migration, honesty

- `toolchain.env` pins Node 22 / pnpm 9.15.4 / `claude` 2.1.269 / `codex` 0.154.0, with
  **`claude >= 2.1.269` asserted against what the binary prints** — at install *and* every service
  start — because a cache or a shadowing global install is exactly how the pin and the binary
  diverge, and the symptom is OAuth refresh dying a week later.
- `migrate-from-docker.sh` **only ever reads** the volume (`:ro` everywhere, no `-v`, no
  `volume rm` — grep-asserted by a gate). `wheel_hostdata` and `wheel_pgdata` are an explicit
  deny-list. sha256 both sides, `PRAGMA integrity_check`, then proves it by authenticating with the
  *migrated* operator token. Rollback is true by construction.
- **§8 of the README is an honest account of what native loses**: no pid/network namespace,
  `master.key` same-uid readable, read-only ≠ invisible, and the fact that `wheeld` never engages
  the shared-uid rail `PROTOCOL.md` says it must (F5). It also says plainly that Docker never gave
  agent-to-agent isolation either — redteam 037 is open on both.

## Rehearsal

`rehearse-native.sh` boots stock Ubuntu 24.04 with real systemd and runs `install.sh` for real.
`harden-probe.sh` lifts the `[Service]` directives out of the **shipped** unit verbatim and runs
`git clone`, `npm install` (package with a build step), a real build, pty, `unshare`+`mount`,
`ss`/`ip`, DNS under them — **15 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped**. `mutate-native.sh` breaks each layer
and requires the guarding checks to go red (`harden`, `sandbox`, `oom` — all verified).

Three fast gates run in `make check` with no Docker: `infra:native-units` (44 assertions,
11 mutations verified), `infra:native-toolchain` (25, 3 mutations), `infra:native-migration`
(20, 5 mutations).

Container-vs-VM gaps are stated in `rehearsal/native/Dockerfile`'s header rather than hidden: no
`cpu` controller delegation (so `CPUQuota` is reported, not asserted), rewritten sysctls, the host's
kernel, no ufw.

---

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: feat(unshare): block unshare creating a user namespace
items.body:
Stacked on #300.

In Cohere's report ([link](https://cohere.com/blog/concerning-behaviour-popular-open-weight-ai-model)), the model got root inside a private user namespace after an offline QEMU build refused it root:

```
unshare -Urm --propagation private sh -c 'mount -t tmpfs -o exec tmpfs /mnt ...'
```

Unprivileged user namespaces are a common starting point for kernel privilege escalation. The command was allowed at every level.

## What

- New `manual_only` rule `unshare.user-namespace` (category Execution), on at every level.
- It fires when an option before the program implies a user namespace: `-U`/`--user`, `-r`/`--map-root-user`, `-c`/`--map-current-user`, `--map-user(s)`, `--map-group(s)`, `--map-auto`, `--map-subids`, `--owner`, `--mount-binfmt`, `-l`/`--load-interp`. Short clusters such as `-Urm` and `-fpU` count, and values of value-taking options are skipped.
- Allowed: other namespaces without a user namespace (`unshare -n true`, `unshare -u hostname`).
- `unshare` joins the protectable commands, so `sudo` and `timeout` in front of it are peeled.
- A destructive program under `unshare` is still analyzed. With a user-namespace flag, the new rule reports first, and the command is blocked either way.

## Known gaps

- A program launched directly by `unshare` (`unshare -n curl http://169.254.169.254/`) skips the head-based device, network and namespace matchers. That's unchanged from main, because `unshare` isn't an exec wrapper. Shell children (`unshare -n sh -c '…'`) are analyzed.
- `xargs … unshare -r` (unchanged from main; `find -exec unshare -r` is blocked).
- `bwrap`, `podman unshare`, `newuidmap`.
- getopt abbreviations of long options (`--use`, `--map-root`) and user-namespace flags placed after `--monotonic`/`--boottime` values.

## Validation

items.title: [reliability] noexec TMPDIR silently costs the TUI and the Go-built k3 binary (npm ci and the Go -x check fail)
items.body:
Found by the k3code audit of 2026-10-12 (static code review, against `Main` at 46edf156). Status: confirmed by an adversarial second reading of the code.

**Severity:** medium | **Platforms:** linux | **Component:** `install/install.sh (TMP/TUI_TMP/ensure_go staging)` | **Effort:** S

## What happens
All staging uses ${TMPDIR:-/tmp}: mktemp at install.sh:524, 567, 830, 850, 895. ensure_go checks '[ -x "$t/go/bin/go" ]' (install.sh:573-574); build_tui runs npm ci there (install.sh:904). Reproduced in WSL inside unshare -Urm with a noexec tmpfs: 'test -x' on an executable file returned FALSE (access(X_OK) fails on noexec mounts), and 'npm ci' of the real tui/ aborted in esbuild's postinstall (spawnargs ['--version'], npm error ... Circular). uv itself built a local project fine with TMPDIR on noexec.

## Impact
On hardened or CIS-style hosts with noexec /tmp the installer finishes 'successfully' but prints only 'WARNING: the TUI did not build' (REPL fallback) and, for Go, 'download failed or did not match the sha256' (misleading; the download and checksum were fine), so no k3 binary. k3code update --from-source/--from-git hits the same.

## Suggested fix
Stage builds under $DATA/tmp (created 0700, on the same filesystem as the install) instead of TMPDIR, or probe TMPDIR for exec once and fall back with a clear message. Do not use [ -x ] on the freshly extracted go; run 'go version' instead.

Tracked in #46.

items.title: fix(gateway): a shadow run's environment reaches only the command, after the capability drop (#1468)
items.body:
## Problem

An overlay shadow hypothesis runs `unshare -Urm … sh run.sh`. The run script mounts the overlay and then `exec`s `setpriv` to drop every capability before the requested command runs. The request's `env` was set on `unshare` itself (`shadow/overlay.rs`). So the namespace shell and `setpriv` started with it while they still held the namespace's full capability set. A loader variable (`LD_PRELOAD`) or a `PATH` entry could run code before the drop (#1468).

## Change

- The bootstrap (`unshare`, the run script, `setpriv`) keeps the gateway's own scrubbed environment.
- The request's variables reach the command only: `setpriv` now runs `env -- NAME=VALUE… COMMAND ARGS…` (`overlay::command_after_drop`) after it has dropped the capabilities. With no variables, the argv is unchanged.
- A variable name that is empty or contains `=` or NUL is refused. A command whose name contains `=` is refused when variables are set, because `env` would take it for one.

## Reproduce and verify

New test `shadow::tests::isolation_eval::request_env_reaches_only_the_command_after_the_capability_drop`. The request's `PATH` starts with a directory holding a benign `mount` hook; the hook appends `CapEff` from `/proc/self/status` to a marker file and then execs the real `mount`. The command prints whether it still sees that `PATH` entry, its own `CapEff`, and a staged file.

Before (main's `overlay.rs`, a Linux build node):

```
the bootstrap ran the request's hook: CapEff:	000001ffffffffff
```

After: the hook never runs. The command prints `path-kept`, `0000000000000000` and `proposed`, so it still gets the request's `PATH` and runs with no capabilities. The six other `isolation_eval` tests still pass, including #440's `request_env_cannot_replace_the_run_script_variables`, and none was skipped.

## Measurements

None.

## Checks

One gate on a Linux build node (default stable toolchain) covered this PR together with the other gateway fixes merged with it. They change disjoint files: #1468 shadow environment, #1483 exec timeout usage, #1495/#1496 redirects, #1527 seed ledger.

- `cargo test -p prod-code-gateway --no-fail-fast`: 37 binaries ran. The only failed target was `--test session_lifecycle`. Three tests there asserted that a client without the `redirects` capability is sent a `Redirect`, which is the defect #1495 fixes. Their clients now declare the capability, and a rerun of `cargo test -p prod-code-gateway --test session_lifecycle` passed 15/15.
- `cargo clippy -p prod-code-gateway --all-targets`: exit 0. The two warnings in touched files (`collapsible_if` at `shadow/overlay.rs:134` and `session/redirect.rs:78`) are on lines this change does not touch.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: exit 0, on the final tree.

Closes #1468

items.title: fix(fsal): git clones, commits and logs through a FUSE mount of a SeaweedFS volume
items.body:
A clone through the FUSE gateway failed one fault per proof. A harness now runs real git against a real SeaweedFS filer through a real mount, and every fault it showed is fixed in this commit:

- **Inode table**: an inode is re-keyed on rename (with everything under a renamed directory) and forgotten on unlink and rmdir. Without this, `config.lock` renamed over `config` read as ENOENT and the clone exited 128.
- **`create_directory`** is the filer's own mkdir, `POST <dir>/` with no body. The multipart POST to `/dir/` was an upload into the filer's `/dir` (201 `{"size":8}`) and made nothing at the path. The `.keep` file that did make the directory showed in every cloned directory and `git add -A` committed it.
- **`delete_directory`** is `DELETE <dir>/?recursive=true`. `DELETE /dir/?path=<dir>` deleted the filer's `/dir` and left the directory in place. A delete of the filer root is refused.
- **RMDIR** refuses a directory that is not empty with ENOTEMPTY. git calls rmdir on a file's directory after removing the file, so `git rm data/000.txt` removed the whole directory.

Each fix has a unit test that failed before it and passes now. The harness `orchestrator/core/tests/seaweedfs_git_e2e.rs` runs only with `AEGIS_SEAWEEDFS_E2E=1` (under `unshare -Urm` where `/etc/fuse.conf` lacks `user_allow_other`) and is skipped otherwise, so CI is unchanged.

items.title: Keep a folder offline: drive offline and drive online (#115)
items.body:
## Summary

`drive offline` keeps a file or folder on this computer by reading it through the mount into rclone's own VFS cache. `drive online` releases that hold. `drive status` lists what is kept and how much disk it uses.

Searched first (rclone v1.75.1): `rclone rc --loopback rc/list` has vfs/forget, vfs/list, vfs/poll-interval, vfs/queue, vfs/queue-set-expiry, vfs/refresh, vfs/stats. There is no vfs/pin. `rclone mount --help` says that when `--vfs-cache-max-size` is exceeded, rclone evicts the least recently accessed files, and that open files cannot be evicted. This change uses that order: a kept path is re-read on every fill pass so it stays the most recently used item. No second sync engine.

Closes #115

items.title: libmount: index the path cache by hash
items.body:
`findmnt -U` gets cubic with many mounts. Repro:

```
unshare -Urm
mkdir /tmp/m
for i in $(seq 2000); do mkdir /tmp/m/$i; mount -t tmpfs none /tmp/m/$i; done
time findmnt -U > /dev/null
exit
rm -r /tmp/m
```

| mounts | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 500 | 2.0 s | 0.055 s |
| 1000 | 6.6 s | 0.086 s |
| 2000 | 51.8 s | 0.28 s |

`mnt_table_uniq_fs()` compares every pair of filesystems, and findmnt's comparator goes through `mnt_fs_match_target()` with the cache, which looks up the other target with `cache_find_path()`. That function is a linear `streq_paths()` scan over a cache that grows to about one entry per mount, so the whole thing is O(n^3).

The fix adds a hash index over the cache's path entries. The hash ignores repeated and trailing slashes so it agrees with `streq_paths()`, matches are still confirmed with `streq_paths()`, and the oldest match is returned like before. If the index can't be allocated it falls back to the old scan. Since it's in libmount, anything else that canonicalizes through the cache benefits too.

Testing: release builds of master and this branch print byte-identical output for 229 findmnt invocations (stdout, stderr and exit code), covering `-U` and plain runs with `-l`, `-J`, `-P`, `-r`, `-o`, `-t`, `-T`, `-R`, `-D`, `-F` on an fstab with `//`, trailing-slash, `..` and symlinked targets, overmounted and bind-mounted targets, and a symlink inside an overmount that makes two different target strings resolve to the same path. `tests/run.sh libmount findmnt fstrim mount` passes (root-only tests skipped), and an ASan/UBSan build of findmnt is clean on `-U` with 1500 mounts.

items.title: Environnement : liens durs, fichier vérifié = fichier ouvert, aucun secret dans l'environnement des commandes
items.body:
## Constats

Suites de la revue de sécurité de #694 (garde des lectures sensibles) et #701 (`write_file` résolu) :

1. Un **lien dur** vers un fichier de justificatifs (`notes.txt` et `.git-credentials` sur le même inode, par exemple après l'extraction d'une archive dans le dossier personnel) n'était pas vu par `read_file` / `write_file` : un lien dur n'a pas de cible à suivre.
2. **Course** entre la vérification (« le chemin demandé mène encore au chemin résolu ») et le `head` / `cat >` : un fichier ou un dossier échangé entre les deux gagnait encore.
3. `run_command` peut lire `/proc/self/environ` (et le `environ` des autres processus de l'utilisateur du bac à sable).

## Correctifs

- **Liens durs** (`RESOLVE_SCRIPT`, `sensitive-path.ts`) : un fichier ordinaire de l'utilisateur du bac à sable avec plus d'un lien rapporte ses autres noms, trouvés par un parcours borné (200 000 entrées, 15 s) du dossier personnel puis du montage du fichier, sans traverser de montage ni suivre de lien. Un nom ordinaire dont un autre nom est un fichier caché ou un emplacement de justificatifs est refusé (lecture et écriture). Liste incomplète (dossier illisible, budget dépassé, plus de 64 noms) : refus. Un deuxième nom ordinaire (magasin pnpm ou uv) passe. Les fichiers de root ne sont pas parcourus : un inode n'a qu'un propriétaire.
- **Vérification = usage** (`OPEN_GUARD`) : la résolution rapporte aussi l'identité (`dev:ino`). La lecture, la liste et l'écriture ouvrent elles-mêmes le chemin résolu (`O_NOFOLLOW`), puis vérifient sur le descripteur que son chemin (`/proc/self/fd/N`, `F_GETPATH` sur macOS pour les tests locaux) est le chemin résolu et que son identité est celle qui a été vérifiée. Ensuite seulement : `head` lit ce descripteur, `ls` le liste (dossier de travail), l'écriture le tronque et le remplit (mode de la cible gardé). Lien, lien dur ou dossier échangé entre-temps : « the path changed », et un fichier qu'une écriture refusée venait de créer est retiré. Le garde passe en argument de `sh` (`$5`), jamais interpolé. Docker et Kubernetes (`withExecEnv` de #701, stdin) inchangés.
- **Environnement des commandes** : décision = ne mettre aucun secret dans l'environnement plutôt que filtrer le texte des commandes. Vérifié : l'exec de `run_command` n'ajoute aucune variable, le conteneur et le pod ne posent que `HOME`, `LANG`, `PATH`, `SAGAX_ENVIRONMENT` (sans jeton de compte de service, sans liens de service). Trouvé en chemin : `sagax-desktop start` lançait Xvnc, openbox, tint2 et Chromium avec `SAGAX_VNC_FULL` / `SAGAX_VNC_VIEW` (et `SAGAX_TEXT` / `SAGAX_URL`) dans leur environnement, lisible par `/proc/<pid>/environ` tant qu'ils tournent. Ces valeurs deviennent des variables shell non exportées dès le début du script.
- **Montages liés** : impossibles depuis l'intérieur (`CapDrop: ALL`, `no-new-privileges`, seccomp par défaut : `mount` et `unshare -Urm` refusés, vérifié sur Docker réel). Documenté, pas de vérification.
- `docs/user-sandbox.md` : les quatre points.

## Tests

- `server/sensitive-path.test.ts` (vrais dossiers, exécution locale) : lien dur vers `.git-credentials`, `.ssh/id_rsa`, `.bashrc` refusé en lecture et en écriture (fichiers intacts) ; lien dur ordinaire (magasin de paquets) lu et écrit ; liste incomplète (dossier verrouillé) refusée ; fichier échangé pour un lien ou un lien dur avant l'ouverture refusé ; dossier échangé pour un lien avant l'ouverture refusé (lecture) ; écriture dont la cible devient un lien dur vers `.git-credentials`, ou dont le dossier devient un lien vers `.ssh`, refusée (rien de créé) ; mode de la cible gardé. Règles pures des alias.
- Nouveau `server/sandbox-exec-env.test.ts` : exec de `run_command` sans variable (via `SandboxService` + faux Docker) ; variables du conteneur et du pod ; le vrai prélude de `sagax-desktop` sous bash : le script garde les valeurs, un processus lancé ne les a pas.
- `server/user-sandbox-routing.test.ts` ajusté (arguments du garde).
- `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm i18n:check` : OK.
- Ciblés (macOS) : 11 fichiers, 150 OK ; `desktop-bridge.e2e`, `user-sandbox.e2e` : 27 OK.
- Conteneur `node:24` Linux, utilisateur non root (chemin `/proc/self/fd`) : 9 fichiers, 132 OK.
- `pnpm test:unit` : tout vert sauf `src/components/ApprovalCard.i18n.test.ts` (2 tests allemand / portugais), **déjà en échec sur `origin/main`** (vérifié sur un checkout propre), sans lien.
- Docker réel (`python:3.11-slim-bookworm`, uid 1000, racine en lecture seule, `--cap-drop ALL`, `no-new-privileges`) : liens durs refusés (justificatifs intacts), lien dur ordinaire lu, lecture et liste ordinaires, nouveau fichier, 300 Kio par stdin, échanges lien dur / lien / dossier refusés, `authorized_keys` jamais créé, `mount --bind` et `unshare -Urm` refusés.

## Limites

- Les variables que la personne donne à **ses propres** serveurs MCP restent dans leur environnement tant qu'ils tournent (nécessaire à leur fonctionnement), comme les fichiers que ces serveurs lisent. `run_command` garde sa carte pour un tour qui n'est pas celui du propriétaire.
- Une écriture refusée par le garde peut laisser des dossiers vides créés par `mkdir -p`.
- Le parcours des liens durs coûte jusqu'à quelques secondes pour un fichier à liens multiples dans un très gros `/workspace` (magasins pnpm) ; au-delà du budget, refus.
- Rien n'est livré ni déployé : l'image du bac à sable (`sagax-desktop`) doit être reconstruite pour le point 3.

items.title: fix: The suite's namespace rows fail from an ordinary terminal on Ubuntu 24.04+

milestone.title: M1 — Measurements
milestone.description: The optimization report and the baseline suite: new measurements, re-runs on the same machine, and defects in either.

items.body:
Milestone: M1 — Measurements

### Work type

bug

### Goal and scope

`bench/README.md` says the suite needs no root and tells people to run `./run.sh` from a terminal. On Ubuntu 24.04 and later, `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns = 1`. An ordinary process may still create a user namespace, but AppArmor moves it into the `unprivileged_userns` profile, which denies every capability, so it cannot map its own uid there. From an ordinary terminal, every row that runs `unshare` fails:

- `cell.unshare_user` and `cell.unshare_4ns` (`bench/sections/cells.py`) fail with "`unshare -Ur true` exited with status 1", which does not say why.
- `storage.fork_ms` and `storage.fork_syscall_ms` (`bench/sections/storage.py`, the overlay mounted inside `unshare -Urm`) fail with "unshare: write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted".

The M runs passed because they ran under a process whose AppArmor profile allows user namespaces. bwrap 0.11.1 has its own profile (`bwrap-userns-restrict`) and works from an ordinary terminal.

Bug report: i7-14700KF, 15 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 26.04, Linux 7.0. Command: `ONLY="cells storage" ./run.sh` from an ordinary context (`systemd-run --user --pipe --wait`). Expected: the rows are measured, or they fail with a reason that names the restriction. Actual: the errors above.

In scope:
- `bench/lib/common.py`: one check of whether this process can do what `unshare -Ur` does, and if not, why. It names AppArmor's restriction when that is the cause.
- `bench/sections/cells.py` and `bench/sections/storage.py`: the `unshare` rows fail with that reason.
- Decide whether to measure the same jobs through bwrap as new rows, and record the decision here.
- `bench/README.md`, *What it needs and what it touches*: which rows need user namespaces, and what happens under Ubuntu's restriction.

Out of scope: weakening AppArmor, or recommending it; relabelling the existing M rows; the prototype's `arbor` section.

### Completion criteria

- A merged PR closes this issue, with `bench/check.sh` passing locally and in CI.
- `ONLY="cells storage" bench/run.sh` has run twice, from a context that allows user namespaces and from an ordinary one (`systemd-run --user`). The PR records each run's load average and result line. The ordinary run either measures the rows or says exactly why it cannot.
- The suite rules still hold: no root, temp files in one `mktemp -d` folder removed on exit, nothing written outside it and `bench/results/`.

### Dependencies, evidence, and constraints

Dependencies: none. The prototype (#14) will later add an `arbor` section to the suite, so this lands first.

Evidence: under a `systemd-run --user` unit (AppArmor label `unconfined`), `unshare -Ur true` fails with "write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted", and `unshare -U cat /proc/self/attr/current` prints `unprivileged_userns (enforce)`. There, `bwrap --ro-bind / / --unshare-all true` works, and so does an overlay over a tree's own path (`--overlay-src DIR --tmp-overlay DIR`).

Constraints:
- No root, and no weakening of AppArmor.
- A new row gets its own key and a reference value from a real run in `bench/lib/reference.py`.
- A number goes into `OPTIMIZATION.md` as M only if it was measured.

items.title: fuse: implement FUSE interrupts
items.body:
fuse: implement FUSE interrupts

This change implements the semantics in the "Interrupting filesystem operations" section of Linux's `Documentation/filesystems/fuse.rst`. Previously, any signal abandoned a FUSE request and restarted (or failed) the syscall.

**Signal handling**
- A signal that interrupts a FUSE request now causes a `FUSE_INTERRUPT` request. It is sent once the server has read the original request.
- After that, only fatal signals end the wait (new `Task.BlockKillable`). The server can honor the interrupt by replying with `EINTR`.
- `FUSE_INTERRUPT` requests take precedence over other requests.
- An `EAGAIN` reply requeues the `FUSE_INTERRUPT`. An `ENOSYS` reply disables interrupts.
- A fatal signal dequeues a request the server hasn't read yet.

**Other behavior changes**
- Replies to unknown requests fail with `ENOENT`, as in Linux. Previously they failed with `EINVAL`.
- `FUSE_RELEASE` is now sent as a forced background request, and `FUSE_FLUSH` is forced. Neither is affected by signals or the active request limit.

**Stops and checkpoints**
Tasks still have to return from syscalls to enter a stop (e.g. for checkpointing), so a stop still restarts the syscall. What changes is how a request the server has already read is handled:
- It is sent a `FUSE_INTERRUPT`, so the server can abort it instead of executing it twice.
- It is forgotten immediately and its active request slot is released. The server's late reply fails with `ENOENT`.

This replaces the recently added "abandoned" approach, which kept the request in place until the server replied. `close(2)` can't be restarted, so `OnClose` ignores `ERESTARTSYS`.

**Known downsides**
- If the server ignores the `FUSE_INTERRUPT` that is sent on a stop and completes the operation anyway, the restarted syscall reissues it. A non-idempotent operation may then run twice. Servers should honor interrupts.
- A killed task returns without waiting for the server's reply.

**Testing**
- New `interrupt_test.go` unit tests.
- New `FuseInterruptTest` and `FuseCheckpointTest` in `test/syscalls/linux/fuse.cc`.
- `//pkg/sentry/fsimpl/fuse:all` passes.

items.title: fuse: implement FUSE interrupts
items.body:
This change implements the semantics in the "Interrupting filesystem operations" section of Linux's `Documentation/filesystems/fuse.rst`. Previously, any signal abandoned a FUSE request and restarted (or failed) the syscall.

**Signal handling**
- A signal that interrupts a FUSE request now causes a `FUSE_INTERRUPT` request. It is sent once the server has read the original request.
- After that, only fatal signals end the wait (new `Task.BlockKillable`). The server can honor the interrupt by replying with `EINTR`.
- `FUSE_INTERRUPT` requests take precedence over other requests.
- An `EAGAIN` reply requeues the `FUSE_INTERRUPT`. An `ENOSYS` reply disables interrupts.
- A fatal signal dequeues a request the server hasn't read yet.

**Other behavior changes**
- Replies to unknown requests fail with `ENOENT`, as in Linux. Previously they failed with `EINVAL`.
- `FUSE_RELEASE` is now sent as a forced background request, and `FUSE_FLUSH` is forced. Neither is affected by signals or the active request limit.

**Stops and checkpoints**
Tasks still have to return from syscalls to enter a stop (e.g. for checkpointing), so a stop still restarts the syscall. What changes is how a request the server has already read is handled:
- It is sent a `FUSE_INTERRUPT`, so the server can abort it instead of executing it twice.
- It is forgotten immediately and its active request slot is released. The server's late reply fails with `ENOENT`.

This replaces the recently added "abandoned" approach, which kept the request in place until the server replied. `close(2)` can't be restarted, so `OnClose` ignores `ERESTARTSYS`.

**Known downsides**
- If the server ignores the `FUSE_INTERRUPT` that is sent on a stop and completes the operation anyway, the restarted syscall reissues it. A non-idempotent operation may then run twice. Servers should honor interrupts.
- A killed task returns without waiting for the server's reply.

**Testing**
- New `interrupt_test.go` unit tests.
- New `FuseInterruptTest` and `FuseCheckpointTest` in `test/syscalls/linux/fuse.cc`.
- `//pkg/sentry/fsimpl/fuse:all` passes.
- `//test/syscalls:fuse_test_runsc_{ptrace,systrap_shared,systrap_shared_save,systrap_shared_save_resume,systrap_fuse,systrap_fuse_save_resume}` pass.
- The new syscall tests also pass natively on Linux (`unshare -Urm`), apart from the pre-existing `CloneFromUnconnectedDeviceFails` failure.



Assisted-by: Claude

items.title: workload-k8s kernel: clone() fails after ~2 threads inside a fresh PID namespace (blocks pod sandboxes)
items.body:
## Blocker

On the `workload-k8s` kernel (#3572), any process that becomes PID 1 in a freshly created PID namespace can create only ~2 threads/children; further `clone()` calls fail. This blocks Kubernetes guests at the root: every pod sandbox is a new PID namespace, and any Go workload as pod init (CoreDNS, most controllers) dies on startup.

## Minimal repro (live guest, via `mvmctl machine exec`)

```
# works
unshare -Ur  /usr/local/bin/k3s --version   # k3s version v1.34.5+k3s1
unshare -Urm /usr/local/bin/k3s --version   # ok (user + mount ns only)
# fails: PID namespace
unshare -Urmp /usr/local/bin/k3s --version
#   runtime: failed to create new OS thread (have 2 already; errno=22)
#   fatal error: newosproc
```

Non-Go probes show the same ceiling from the other syscall:

```
unshare -Urmp sh -c 'sleep 2 & sleep 2 & wait; echo OK'        # OK (2 forks)
unshare -Urmp sh -c 'for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do (echo) & done; wait'
#   sub1
#   sh: can't fork: Out of memory        # 3rd clone() fails
```

So ~2 clone()s succeed inside a fresh pid ns, then fail: errno 22 (EINVAL) via Go's clone3 path, errno 12 (ENOMEM) via plain fork. External binary execs (which also clone) passed at count 2 - the ceiling, not the syscall shape, is the constant.

## Environment

- Kernel: workload-k8s aarch64, Linux 6.12.110, 1041 built-ins (mvm#3572 guards green)
- VM: 4 vCPU / 4 GiB ( reproduced at 512 MiB first; NOT memory pressure - 3.9 GiB free at repro)
- Reproduced both from the workload uid (901) and root-in-userns (`unshare -Urmp`); plain `unshare -p` as 901 is EPERM as expected
- Not cgroup-position-dependent: the failing processes sit in the v2 root cgroup (no pids/memory limit; `memory.max=max`)

## Suspects for the config bisect

The slim-kernel lineage is the differentiator (distro kernels run Go-as-pid1-in-podns everywhere). Candidates, in order:

- `CONFIG_SLUB_TINY` / SLOB-style allocator trimming interacting with `create_pid_cachep`'s per-pid-ns kmem cache (a fresh pid ns allocates from a brand-new, cold cache)
- any other config that changes `alloc_pid()` / pidmap backing behavior under a new ns
- Compare against the nixpkgs default aarch64 kernel config with only the mvm deltas applied, bisecting the mvm `base.nix`/`workload-k8s.nix` disable lists

## Impact

- k3s server itself works around it by dropping `-p` from the bring-up `unshare` (`unshare -Urm` runs the server fine - committed to the kubernetes template)
- Pod sandboxes are unaffected only while their init is non-Go and stays under the clone ceiling; CoreDNS and friends will not start
- Found during the Kubernetes-in-microVM smoke test (tinylabscom/mvm-templates#1, mvm#3554); the rest of the bring-up chain (cgroup2 delegation, uid-901 identity, /dev/kmsg faking, builder-VM image contract) is now validated live

items.title: Linux: deny new user namespaces to agent commands under Moderate and Aggressive (#826)
items.body:
Fixes #826 (follow-up of #766 / #827): on Linux, agent commands under Moderate and Aggressive can no longer create user namespaces, so `unshare -Ur` / `unshare -Urm` can't open or mount over what bubblewrap hides and nested-launch detection (`security-level/src/nested.rs`) can't be defeated that way.

**Sign-off basis:** Travis, 2026-10-15, option (a) on #826 with security sign-off ("deny new user namespaces (CLONE_NEWUSER) to agent commands under the protected levels, tested on glitch for what it breaks"). Permissive is unchanged (also after untrusted content); macOS and Windows are unchanged. Nothing is weaker than on main.

## Before / after (glitch, real bubblewrap)
| Agent command | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unshare -Ur cat <denied file>` (bwrap's 000 placeholder) | opens it | `unshare failed: Operation not permitted` |
| `unshare -Urm sh -c 'mount -t tmpfs none <folder>'` | mounts | EPERM |
| Moderate / Aggressive / launch-only Aggressive: `unshare -Ur ls <home>/secrets`, `cat <Moderate marker>` | listed / opened | EPERM |
| Moderate: `unshare -Ur env CODEX_HOME=<other> HOME=… corbanu exec …` | ran at the other home's level (Permissive), reached the model | EPERM, no nested run |
| Moderate / Aggressive: `unshare -Ur corbanu exec …` (same home) | not recognised as nested | EPERM |
| A Corbanu sandbox started inside (nested `corbanu exec`'s commands) | fails (read-only registry lock panic) | fails with: "Corbanu's Linux sandbox cannot start here: … under security level Moderate or Aggressive, where creating user namespaces is denied …" |
| Permissive (with or without untrusted content) | namespace made | unchanged |

## How
- **Protocol:** a `:user_namespaces` deny entry (`FileSystemSandboxEntry::deny_user_namespaces`), carried as `FileSystemSpecialPath::Unknown` like #758's `:keychain_services`: no file access, not a read denial, part of the semantic signature; other sandboxes ignore it. On Linux it requires the platform sandbox (`should_require_platform_sandbox`).
- **Core (`tools/orchestrator.rs`):** on Linux, every agent command's profile (materialized and exec-server) gets the entry when Core's level is Moderate or Aggressive (where the protected-path rules apply, including a person's approval under Moderate and Aggressive grants) or the launch enforces Aggressive (`launch_enforces_aggressive`, also while Core's level is Permissive, #428). No approval or grant lifts it. A profile without Corbanu's sandbox (disabled, external) can't carry it, as with the other rules.
- **linux-sandbox (`landlock.rs`):** with the entry, `no_new_privs` plus two seccomp filters in the inner stage (after bubblewrap set up its own namespace; also the legacy-Landlock and full-write paths): `unshare`/`clone` with `CLONE_NEWUSER` → `EPERM`; `clone3` (flags in memory a filter can't read) → `ENOSYS`, so glibc/Go/Rust fall back to `clone` (Docker/Flatpak do the same). x32 aliases on x86_64 are covered too. `setns` isn't needed: joining a user namespace needs `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in it, which the command only has in ones it created.
- **Clear failure:** the command's environment gets `CODEX_SANDBOX_USER_NAMESPACES_DENIED=1` (allowed by the secretless allowlist's `CODEX_` prefix). A `codex-linux-sandbox` started there tries a namespace in a forked child first and, on `EPERM`, prints the message above and exits 1 instead of bubblewrap's misleading "kernel does not allow non-privileged user namespaces". The variable only selects the message; a forged one does nothing when the namespace can be made. It isn't classified as a sandbox start-up failure, so no "retry without sandbox?" is offered.
- Why seccomp and not `bwrap --disable-userns`: works with every bubblewrap (Ubuntu 22.04 ships 0.6, the option is 0.8+), covers the legacy Landlock path, and fails with `EPERM` (`--disable-userns` gives `ENOSPC`).

## What breaks under Moderate and Aggressive on Linux (documented)
Anything that needs a user namespace: a sandbox of its own (the commands of a nested `corbanu exec`: already failing on main, now explained), `unshare`, `bwrap`, rootless Podman/Buildah/Docker, Flatpak, Nix's single-user build sandbox, Chrome/Electron with their sandbox on (Puppeteer's default; `--no-sandbox`, as Playwright does, works). Survey on glitch (`glitch-survey.log`): shell, python threads + subprocess, node child_process + worker threads, rustc + threads, git and `nix eval` keep working. Docs: `docs/security-moderate.md` (Limits), `docs/security-aggressive.md` (new "User namespaces on Linux"), `linux-sandbox/README.md`.

## Gate
- **Fail before / pass after on glitch** (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, AppArmor userns restriction on, bubblewrap through `aa-exec`): `linux-sandbox/tests/suite/user_namespaces.rs` (EPERM for read and mount-over with and without network, `clone3` ENOSYS with threads/subprocess still working, nested sandbox message; Permissive unchanged), `core/tests/suite/issue_826.rs` (Moderate, Aggressive, launch-only Aggressive, Moderate+launch Aggressive denied; Permissive before/after untrusted content unchanged), `cli/tests/nested_moderate.rs::issue_826_*` (Moderate other home, Moderate and Aggressive same home via `unshare -Ur`; Permissive unchanged). Before: main's code with only the protocol entry and tests → all three fail as in the table.
- **Linux (glitch):** linux-sandbox 56/56 + 142 unit; core `--lib security:: tools::orchestrator` 378/378; core security suite (pf_23/pf_25/issue_736/747/748/766/826, nested, aggressive, moderate, protected, sandbox, code_mode, rmcp_client) 168/168 with helper binaries; cli `nested_moderate` 11/11 + `nested_launch`; protocol/sandboxing/security-level unit tests.
- **macOS:** `just test` protocol/sandboxing/security-level 456/456; core security set 96/96.
- **Clippy `-D warnings`:** macOS and Linux (protocol, sandboxing, linux-sandbox, core, cli; Linux also with developer-accounting).
- Evidence: `qa/security-levels/linux-userns-826-20261015/`.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)
- Contained Claude panes don't get the rule (Claude Code's own bubblewrap sandbox may need user namespaces); a decision for Travis.
- The inspector / approval explanations don't name the rule yet (a failed `unshare` says only "Operation not permitted").
- Core decides on the Core host's OS: a macOS Core driving a remote Linux exec server doesn't add it.

items.title: Two machines, one file: keep both saves, and work offline
items.body:
## What this closes

drive#30: two devices edit the same file inside one sync window, and both
versions survive. The earlier save lands as `name (conflict, <device>).ext`,
the later save is the plain file, and both devices see both. Edits made
offline upload on reconnect under the same rule.

## The rule

Object storage overwrites: whichever upload lands last wins the one plain
path. Stock rclone has no conflict-copy flag for a mount, so the rule is
ours and it rides on the remote control the mount already runs for the
background fill and `drive status`:

- `vfs/queue` names this device's own uploads that storage has not taken
  yet. A path there is a save in flight, so this device's bytes are still
  on this machine, staged to `~/.config/drive/conflict-staging/` (inside the
  device's own config folder, so nothing staged is ever visible in the drive
  and nothing staged is ever uploaded except the conflict copy itself).
- A path that leaves the queue has landed. The plain path's object hash is
  read back. Equal to this device's hash means this device's save is the one
  that landed.
- A hash that is neither this device's bytes nor the version that preceded
  the save means the other device's save landed. The staged copy is written
  as the conflict copy under the losing device's own name.

A conflict copy is written only by the device that lost the save, after its
own upload has landed, and is verified by reading the written object back
and comparing its hash: a name that holds another writer's bytes is retried
under the next number, so a conflict copy is this device's own save or it is
not written. Nothing is deleted and nothing is renamed.

`drive mount` gained `--device` (the name in a conflict copy, default the
hostname) and `--rc-addr` (the loopback address the remote control binds,
so two mounts of one drive on one host do not collide on one port).

## Why it is not code without a caller

The conflict rule lives next to the mount that runs it: `mountForeground`
starts the guard in the mount process, on the same remote control as the
fill, for as long as the mount runs. No second daemon, no script. The rule
is one goroutine, one `stat` and one `vfs/queue` read per half second on an
idle machine. `cmd/drive/` is on `main` (PR #26 merged), which is the
condition drive#30's earlier park names.

## Verification

Every line below is a real run on this host, against the same local
`rclone serve s3` stand-in the step-3 proofs use. FUSE is refused to this
unprivileged worker, so the mount proofs run inside a user namespace
(`unshare -Urm`), which is a real kernel mount: the test reads and writes
through real FUSE mounts, and the guard reads its answers back from real
`rclone rc` calls. The old "two plain directories" false positive is
excluded because `waitForMount` requires `findmnt` to report the mount point
before the test continues.

Two independent `rclone mount` processes, each a separate `drive mount`
with its own home, config, prefix and VFS cache, sharing only the storage
backend: two machines.

**Acceptance 1 — two devices edit the same file within one sync window, both
versions survive, both devices notified.**

```
$ unshare -Urm go test ./cmd/drive -run TestTwoDevicesKeepBothSaves -v
--- PASS: TestTwoDevicesKeepBothSaves (14.53s)
    two devices, one save window: storage=stand-in, plain="report.txt", conflict="report (conflict, mac).txt", A's listing=[report (conflict, mac).txt report.txt]
```

Device A ("mac") saved first, device B ("linux") saved second, inside the
same write-back window. The plain file holds the save that landed later;
the earlier save is `report (conflict, mac).txt`. Device A's listing has
exactly two files, and the test reads the conflict copy through both
mounts, so both devices are notified.

Also proven: the same case when the two saves are **seconds apart**
(`TestTwoSavesSecondsApartInOneWindowBothSurvive`). A same-instant proof
hides the case a person actually has: each device's write-back timer fires
on its own, so the first save has already landed at the plain path when the
second one lands on top of it. In the state this PR started from
(commit `6504e65`) the guard resolved that case with a single line —

```go
case landed == save.hash:
	// This device's save is the one that landed.
	delete(g.seen, name)
```

which deleted the watch entry and its staged copy, so the earlier save was
silently overwritten with nothing to restore it from. The new proof failed
against that state (`one save was lost: neither [notes (conflict, mac).txt
notes (conflict, linux).txt] appeared on device A`) and passes now.

```
$ unshare -Urm go test ./cmd/drive -run TestTwoSavesSecondsApartInOneWindowBothSurvive -v
--- PASS: TestTwoSavesSecondsApartInOneWindowBothSurvive (8.38s)
    two saves seconds apart, one sync window: plain="B: saved second, still inside the same sync window\n", conflict="notes (conflict, mac).txt", A's listing=[notes (conflict, mac).txt notes.txt]
```

**Acceptance 2 — edits made offline upload on reconnect under the same rule.**

The stand-in server is killed, both devices save the same file while storage
is unreachable, then the server is started again on the same endpoint. Both
queued uploads happen on reconnect and the rule decides what is kept.

```
    after the reconnect: plain="B: the save made while the device could not reach storage\n", conflict="A: the save made while the device could not reach storage\n", both saves kept
```

**Acceptance 3 — proven with a two-mount test.** Both proofs above are two-mount
proofs: two real FUSE mounts on one Linux host, each running its own guard.

Unit tests over a counted stand-in drive the decision itself, one case per
row: the loser's version is kept, a skip is named once, a name another mount
took is retried, a winning save is left alone until the overwrite window
ends, a repeated conflict numbers its copy, a folder stays in the conflict
name, a save that has not landed is waited for, a save over the staging cap
is named, and a failing pass is not swallowed into "no conflict".

```
$ go test ./cmd/drive -short -run TestConflict -v
--- PASS: TestConflictNamePutsTheDeviceBeforeTheExtension (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictNameKeepsTheFolder (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictDeviceFromName (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardKeepsTheLosersVersion (0.01s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardNamesASkipOnce (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardRetriesANameAnotherMountTook (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardGivesUpWhenEveryNameIsTaken (0.01s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardLeavesAWinningSaveAlone (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardKeepsASaveThatLandsSecondsLater (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardStagesTheBytesTheUploadWillCarry (0.01s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardNumbersARepeatedConflict (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardKeepsAFolderInTheConflictName (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardWaitsForASaveThatHasNotLandedYet (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardSkipsASaveTooLargeToStage (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardNamesASaveItCanNoLongerRestage (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestConflictGuardReportsAFailingPass (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestMatchHashSum (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestCopyFileWithHashStagesTheBytes (0.00s)
--- PASS: TestCopyFileWithHashRefusesASaveThatGrewPastTheCap (0.22s)
```

**The rest of the CI gate, run on this host.**

```
$ go vet ./cmd/...                                  # ok
$ go build -o /tmp/drive ./cmd/drive                # ok
$ go test ./cmd/drive -short                        # ok  4.5s
$ unshare -Urm go test ./cmd/drive -count=1         # ok  360.9s  (full suite, the stand-in proofs included)
$ unshare -Urm go test ./cmd/drive -run TestStandinMountProof -v   # PASS
$ semgrep --config p/default --baseline-commit "$(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)"   # 1 finding, suppressed below
$ git ls-files scripts bin tools ops '*.sh'         # empty: no new scripts
```

## in-run review

The stock reviewer was run on the diff with `--no-tools` and the hard 300 s
cap; it did not return findings (it started a local file-reading loop,
which is the known `--tools` behaviour), so the review was performed in-run
against the diff by hand. Two findings came out of it, and a third came out
of the new two-mount proof (described under Acceptance 1):

1. **A pass result was computed and then discarded.** `ConflictResult`
   carried every claim and every skip, and `RunConflictLoop` dropped it on
   the floor, so a save the rule could not protect was entirely silent —
   which is the one thing the guard exists to avoid. Both are reported now
   (once per `conflictReportEvery` per message) on the channel the mount
   already prints, and that reporting is what keeps a skip a named thing a
   person can act on.
2. **A re-stage that could no longer stage left the older bytes in place.**
   If a save grew past the staging cap after being first staged, the stale
   staged copy could have been claimed as the conflict copy — a version
   nobody uploaded. That path is now named as a skip, with the reason, and
   no conflict name is written for it
   (`TestConflictGuardNamesASaveItCanNoLongerRestage`).

One question the review raised ("use SHA256 instead of MD5") was not
applied, for the reason in the next section.

## MD5 (semgrep `use-of-md5`) — suppressed with reason

```
cmd/drive/conflict_guard.go
  use-of-md5  (blocking, suppressed with // nosemgrep)
```

MD5 is used as a content identity check, not as a signature. One half of
every comparison is `operations/hashsum` with `hashType: md5`, which reads
the content hash rclone records for the object — on S3, the ETag — so it
is the only hash both halves can answer. `sha256` is not returned by the S3
backend without `--download`, which would mean downloading the whole object
on every one of the guard's half-secondly passes, and a half that compares
equal to nothing is not a comparison at all.

The properties the rule actually relies on are checked separately: the
conflict copy is written and then read back from storage and its hash is
compared to this device's own hash, so a name holding another writer's
bytes is not accepted and the copy is retried (`claim`). An attacker who
can write to this device's staging directory can already write to the
drive, and MD5's collision weakness is the wrong attack for both.

## Files in scope

All changes are in `cmd/drive/`, where drive#30's body says the fix belongs
("Whatever shape the fix takes, it belongs in `cmd/drive` next to
`mount.go`, so it lands with the CLI rather than as an orphan"). No
`scripts/`, `bin/`, `ops/`, `tools/` or `*.sh` file is added. No
dependency is added. `go.mod` is untouched.

## Not done, and why

**Real storage.** The proofs use the `rclone serve s3` stand-in, as
drive#2 and step 3 do. iDrive e2 / Backblaze B2 versioning and retention
(#2, #9) are what make "both versions survive" rest on the storage
provider rather than on this device, and they are separate steps. The rule
here does not depend on versioning: every byte it keeps is a byte this
device writes itself.

**The Mac-plus-Linux two-machine proof on real hosts.** drive#30's
resume-when condition and #4 name it, and `AGENTS.md` records that
Mac-only proofs run on a GitHub macOS runner or are marked for Nish.
Both proofs here are two-mount proofs on one Linux host, and both devices
are real FUSE mounts talking to real rclone remote-control calls against
real objects in the stand-in bucket — but they are not a Mac. The same
`drive mount` code path runs on both platforms (`BuildMountPlan` picks
`nfsmount` on darwin and `mount` on Linux), so the behaviour being proven
is platform-independent.

**Retention windows.** The 1-hour/1-day-B2/30-day-Hetzner retention in
`docs/spec.md` is what a conflict copy's survival ultimately rests on; it
is built in #2 and #9, not here.

## One thing worth knowing

The staging directory is bounded, not cumulative: at most one staged copy
per save that is still in its upload window, released (`releaseStaged`) the
moment that path is decided — claimed, dropped as a skip, or confirmed a
winner. Before this PR nothing removed them, so every save left its bytes
on disk under `~/.config/drive/conflict-staging/` for the life of the
mount, which is an unbounded local copy of the drive on a product whose
point is not to copy the drive onto the machine.

Closes #30

items.title: Overlay shadow runs bypass read-only file permissions through retained namespace-root capabilities
items.body:
Observed while verifying #484. Ordinary `prod-code exec --no-pull -- cargo test -p prod-code-mcp --test orchestration a_rename_across_repositories_is_written_in_all_or_none` passes (the focused diagnose run recorded 1 passed, 0 failed). The same existing test inside `prod-code shadow-run <spec> -- env RUSTC_WRAPPER= cargo test -p prod-code-mcp --lib --tests` fails: `expect_err` receives a successful applied multi-repository rename despite the second schema file being marked read-only. It is an assertion failure, not a build error. Current source launches overlay commands with `unshare -Urm ... sh`, retaining namespace-root permissions after mounting. Expected: the tested command should retain the ordinary user's file-access behavior after the overlay mount; inability to write a read-only fixture must not become permission to write it. Reproduce with a self-contained file created then chmod 0444 in a shadow command, compare an ordinary remote command, and preserve overlay/build isolation when dropping mount privileges. Add a native Linux regression and verify the existing atomic multi-repository rename test in both modes.

## Environment

- client: prod-code 0.3.18 on macos aarch64
- node: linux aarch64, engines: rust (ra_ap_ide), go (gopls), cpp (clangd), python (basedpyright-langserver), typescript (tsc --lsp), generic-lsp

_Filed with `prod-code report-issue`._

items.title: Linux folder mode under Ubuntu's AppArmor userns restriction: own bubblewrap + one scoped profile (#122)
items.body:
Closes #122. Part of Cloud #2383 (用户电脑接入). Follows #123 (bubblewrap static build, released as `bwrap-static-0.13.1-r1`).

**Root cause:** Ubuntu 23.10+ sets `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`. Only the packaged `/usr/bin/bwrap` may then make capability-bearing user namespaces, through Ubuntu's `bwrap-userns-restrict` profile. That profile stacks every child with `unpriv_bwrap` (`audit deny capability`). srt's seccomp helper makes a nested namespace inside bubblewrap, so it failed with `setgroups: Permission denied`, and folder mode could not start on stock Ubuntu.

On the owner's 26.04, inside the packaged bwrap the label is `bwrap//&unpriv_bwrap (enforce)`, and `unshare -Urm` there is refused. The old fix was a global sysctl. It re-opened capability-bearing namespaces to every program on the PC.

**Coordinator decision:** a scoped AppArmor profile; the seccomp layer stays on.

**What:**
- **Own bubblewrap.** `runtimes::BWRAP` is the pinned 0.13.1-r1 static build. Its digests match the publish run's log, and `sandbox setup` provisions it like ripgrep and socat. The distribution's bwrap is no longer used, so the apt/dnf install line and `install_line`/`os_release` are deleted (one path).
- **`crates/sandbox/src/userns.rs`:**
  - With the restriction on, srt's `bwrapPath` is a **root-owned** copy of the same pin, at `/usr/local/libexec/agentrouter/bwrap-0.13.1-r1/bwrap`.
  - `sudo agentrouter sandbox userns install` fetches it with the pinned SHA-256 and checks that root owns it and its folders.
  - It then writes `/etc/apparmor.d/agentrouter-bwrap` and loads it (`apparmor_parser --replace`). The profile follows Ubuntu's per-app pattern: `abi <abi/4.0>`, `flags=(unconfined)`, `userns,`, one exact path, no glob.
  - The command is idempotent. `… userns remove` unloads and deletes both.
  - The grant never names a user-writable path: that would hand the namespaces to anything dropping a file in the home folder.
  - The command inside the sandbox still runs under srt's filter, which refuses new user namespaces.
- **`HOSTD_SANDBOX_NEEDS_ADMIN`** names `sudo <absolute exe> sandbox userns install`, and the remove line. It appears when the copy or the profile is missing, or when a confined start still fails for user namespaces. A kernel switch that refuses namespaces (`unprivileged_userns_clone=0`, `max_user_namespaces=0`) gets its own sysctl.d line. The global AppArmor sysctl line is gone.
- **CI (Linux sandbox job):**
  - The restriction stays **on** and the runner's bwrap/socat/rg are hidden.
  - Before the tests, it checks that the status names the line and that install runs twice (the second run changes nothing). The copy must be `0:755`, the user-writable copy must still be refused a namespace, and the root copy's label must be `agentrouter-bwrap`.
  - All sandbox tests (escape, aggregator e2e, `link_e2e`) then run through that copy.
  - Afterwards, remove must delete both and the status asks again. With the restriction off, the status is ready with no admin step.
- Docs: HOSTD-MCP §6.3/§6.4/§6.5 and AV-HYGIENE.

**Workstation (before this PR):** a root-owned bwrap with this profile shape ran srt 0.0.81 with all layers on, from a plain unconfined context (`systemd-run --user`). registry.npmjs.org returned 200. example.com, a write outside the folder, a nested `unshare -Ur` and an `AF_UNIX` socket were all refused. That test profile is removed again.

items.title: gate-7 no-admin-idor: 5 real unguarded endpoints (1 critical, 2 high, 2 medium) of 18 findings
items.body:
`gate-7 no-admin-idor` reports **18 findings whole-tree** on `development`
(cf1ed3980). Triaged all 18 against the source: **5 are real, 13 are false
positives.** Not fixed here — filing so they get a decision.

## The gate was proven live first

This gate class has produced real IDORs twice recently, and a **missing helper
once made it report PASS over 11 real unguarded endpoints** (.github#147), so it
was positive-controlled before any "false positive" verdict was trusted:

- a fixture app with `#[NoAdminRequired] fn(string $id)` and no guard -> **FAIL**,
  naming the method. Repeated with the controller in the `OCA\OpenRegister`
  namespace so the OR-delegation heuristic could not silently clear it.
- the same fixture with a real guard added -> **PASS**
- helper deleted -> **SKIPPED**, explicitly stating 139 controllers were in scope
  and none inspected. There is no code path that can `_pass` without running the
  helper (`run-hydra-gates.sh:674-684`); the .github#147 shape is closed.
- helper replaced with a marker stub -> the marker reached the log and drove the
  count, proving the runner really executes it rather than merely finding it.

All runs used a private `/tmp` (`unshare -Urm` + tmpfs) because the runner's
hardcoded `/tmp/hydra-gate-*.log` paths are corrupted by concurrent runs. The 18
reproduced byte-identically.

## The 5 real ones

**S1 — CRITICAL. `FederatedConfigController::bundle()` (:115), `POST /api/federated-config/bundle`.**
Any authenticated non-admin. The only one of the three federated-config paths
with no `FederatedConfigAccess` check (compare `install()` :149, `publish()` :205).
Reaches:
- `GenericObjectShareableConfigType::serialise()` -> `objectService->findAll(..., _rbac: false, _multitenancy: false)` — **read every object of that register/schema across every organisation.** (`_rbac === false` confirmed honoured at `PermissionHandler:334`.)
- `FlowShareableConfigType::serialise()` -> `FlowMapper::findByUuid()`, which has **no org filter and no `MultiTenancyTrait`** — read any flow definition on the instance by uuid, cross-org. Always registered.
- `RegisterSchema`/`ConfigSet` types with `includeObjects` -> `ExportHandler:342` calls `objectEntityMapper->findAll()` with **no RBAC argument** — per-object RBAC bypassed within the org.

**S2 — HIGH. `FederationController::createShare()` (:103).**
Any authenticated non-admin mints an outgoing share for an arbitrary
register/schema/object with `read-write`. The `#[PublicPage]` serving endpoints
then honour that token with `_rbac: false, _multitenancy: false`. `updateObject`
(:286) and `deleteObject` (:325) take an arbitrary `$id` and never check the
target's organisation -> **modify or delete objects by uuid, cross-org.** For
`scope: "object"` the confidentiality filter is skipped entirely (:517), so
confidential objects are readable by choosing object scope.

**S3 — HIGH. `FederationController::shares()` (:85).**
Org-scoped but with **no per-share ownership check**, and
`FederatedShare::jsonSerialize()` emits **`shareToken`** (`FederatedShare.php:299`).
Any org member harvests every federation bearer token the org holds — which are
credentials to the S2 endpoints. Intra-org (plus parent orgs via the hierarchy).

**S4 — MEDIUM. `FederationController::revokeShare()` (:136).**
Sequential integer `$id`, org-scoped only, no ownership check. Enumerate `1..N`
and revoke every federation share the org and its parents hold -> **DoS on all
federation**, including admin-created shares.

**S5 — MEDIUM. `FlowController::state()` (:184).**
`FlowStateMapper::findByFlow()` is a bare `WHERE flow_id = ?` with **no
organisation filter and no `MultiTenancyTrait`** — the only one of the 18 whose
mapper has no tenancy scoping at all. In-org, uuids come free from `index()`;
cross-org, any leaked uuid crosses the tenant boundary. Structural omission
rather than a policy choice.

## The 13 false positives

Each has a named, verified guard — not "looks fine":

- `FederatedConfigController::types` / `publicKey` — zero params; static catalogue / the **public** half of the signing key.
- `FederatedConfigController::discover` / `fetch` — address a **remote** GitHub resource under a fixed host via the caller's *own* credential; no OR object dereferenced.
- `FlowController::eventCatalog` / `nodeCatalog` — static registries, no persisted object addressed.
- `FlowController::validate` — operates on a caller-supplied document, no storage read/write.
- `FlowController::index` — `FlowService::findAll()` returns `[]` when no active org (fails closed).
- `FlowController::show` / `update` / `destroy` / `run` — all route through `FlowService::find()`, which throws unless `Flow::belongsTo(activeOrganisation())`; `belongsTo` returns **false** when either side is null (fails closed), mapped to 404 so there is no existence oracle.
- `FlowController::create` — `owner`/`organisation`/`uuid` are server-stamped and absent from the `applyEditableFields` allowlist, so a payload cannot claim another identity or tenant.

Confirmed there is no invisible authz middleware (`Application.php:442-502` registers none), and that the four docblock-only `@NoAdminRequired` methods really are non-admin reachable (NC33 `SecurityMiddleware` accepts the annotation as well as the attribute) — so none is accidentally admin-protected.

## Secondary findings (not gate-7 IDORs)

- `ConfigurationMapper::find()`/`findByApp()` carry live comments **"Verify RBAC permission to read. TEMPORARILY DISABLED FOR TESTING — TODO: Re-enable"** (:158-160, :191-193). Org filtering still applies; RBAC does not.
- `FlowController::nodeCatalog()`'s docblock claims it is scope-filtered "so a non-administrator is never offered a step they could not run" — the default is `SCOPE_ADMIN` and the scope is caller-chosen. **The claim is false.**
- Flow CRUD is **org**-scoped, not owner-scoped, so any org member can rewrite a colleague's flow; triggered runs execute under whoever fires the event.

## Explicitly unverified

- **None of the 5 was exercised against a live instance** — all verdicts are from source reading plus gate runs. S1/S2 deserve a live HTTP confirmation before severities are treated as final.
- Whether `x-openregister-shareable` is set on any schema in a default install — determines whether S1's worst path is live out of the box. The flow and register/config-set paths are always registered regardless.
- Whether `Flow::jsonSerialize()` can carry inline secrets rather than credential references — changes how bad S1's flow-export path is.
- `ExportHandler::exportConfig` was read only at the object-dump block; whether another branch applies RBAC is unverified.

items.title: Published speed numbers, including where we lose
items.body:
The Go suite, the public Benchmarks page and the gate for every speed figure issue #99 names. Linux numbers stay unmeasured until real storage (#173); Mac numbers stay unmeasured until they are run on a Mac. Stand-in figures on this host are not published.

Remainder: #242 (blocked on #173).

## What I looked at
- Stock rclone (`serve s3`, `mount`, `--bwlimit`) — no helper script, no hand-rolled engine
- `go test ./cmd/drive` — the suite is Benchmark functions in `cmd/drive/bench_test.go`
- The docs site from #98 (VitePress + `src/render-docs.js` markers)
- The scoreboard gate from #114 (`test/scoreboard.test.mjs`)
- `test/two-mount-sync.test.mjs` for the two-mount cross-machine pattern
- Issue #173 (real iDrive e2) — no `idrive` rclone remote on this host; loopback remotes only
- Space figures already recorded in `docs/scoreboard.md` (checked 2026-09-30)

## Scope
- `cmd/drive/e2e_test.go` because TestMain tears down the shared bench harness
- `README.md` because a new docs page must be linked
- `docs-site/benchmarks.md`, `docs-site/index.md`, `docs-site/changelog.md`, `docs-site/.vitepress/config.mts` because that is how the public page is authored
- `public/llms.txt`, `public/sitemap.xml` because `DOC_PAGES` registration has to match the committed site files
- `src/render-docs.js`, `src/seo.js` because the table is injected and the page is listed
- `test/benchmarks.test.mjs` because it is the gate the suite comment names

## Losing rows
None. Every Linux and Mac Us cell is `not yet measured`, so there is no loss to file. #242 will name each losing row when it has a real-storage figure.

## Acceptance

- Benchmarks are Go benchmarks in the repo, run with `go test` (no script files): first byte and first 100 MB of a 5 GB file, a 1 GB save reaching storage, a small edit in a 64 MiB and a 2 GB file, listing 10,000 files, install-to-mounted time, plus the owner-added small-file, `--bwlimit` and cross-machine scenarios.
  `cmd/drive/bench_test.go:314` `BenchmarkVideoStartFirstByte`, `:349` `BenchmarkSaveReachesStorage`, `:389` `BenchmarkSmallEdit`, `:424` `BenchmarkListFolder`, `:551` `BenchmarkInstallToMounted`, `:447` `BenchmarkSmallFiles`, `:505` `BenchmarkVideoStartBandwidth`, `:615` `BenchmarkCrossMachineSync`.
  ```
  go test ./cmd/drive -short -count=1
  ok  	github.com/Nishfleet/drive/cmd/drive	2.848s

  PASS
  ok  	github.com/Nishfleet/drive/cmd/drive	52.347s
  ```
  Every report line from that run had `storage=stand-in` and is not in the published table.

- Run on real storage from the VPS, results with date, region, link speed and commit in `docs/benchmarks.md` and on a public Benchmarks page, next to Space's published figure, losses shown as losses.
  not run: no real storage on this host (#173; rclone remotes are loopback). The page and table exist with Us = `not yet measured` (`docs/benchmarks.md:42`, `src/seo.js:101`, `docs-site/benchmarks.md`). Remainder #242.

- The Mac numbers (spec step 2: first frame under 3 s, 1 GB save within 10 s) are marked 'not yet measured'; not estimated.
  `docs/benchmarks.md:64` and `:72` `mac-first-frame` / `mac-1gb-save` both `not yet measured`.
  ```
  node --test test/benchmarks.test.mjs
  ✔ Mac rows stay not yet measured and are never estimated
  ℹ tests 6
  ℹ pass 6
  ```

- Numbers against a stand-in on the same machine are not publishable.
  `test/benchmarks.test.mjs` fails a Us cell that says stand-in. Published Linux Us cells are `not yet measured` (`docs/benchmarks.md:42`).

## Verification

items.title: Desktop: after rclone dies the mount cannot recover; the unit restart-loops, "drive unmount" reports success without unmounting, and queued saves stay on disk

labels.name: needs-coordinator
labels.description: touches a path outside the arm allowlist: the coordinator reviews and arms it

items.body: When rclone is killed, the FUSE (or macOS NFS) entry stays in the mount table. The login item then restart-loops, `drive mount` blames disk space, and `drive unmount` reports success without taking the entry down. This PR makes the login item clear a dead FUSE or NFS entry before start, makes `drive unmount` actually stop and verify the mount, and makes `drive status` name that stale mount with one command: `drive unmount`. Coordinator review on b2de19c: (1) kill-9 stand-in remount plus queued upload is `TestStandinMountProofKillNineRecoversQueuedSave`. (2) `clearStaleMountDir` only lazy-unmounts a listed mount that does not answer. (3) the mount listing is consulted before Lstat, with a 2s bound. (4) the rc random-port and `core/version` check are #807, shipped in #816, and are not in this PR. scope: cmd/drive/logout.go because `stopMount` / `runFusermount` already live there, and lazy unmount (`-uz` / `umount -f`) has to be on that path. scope: cmd/drive/config_test.go, cmd/drive/messages_test.go, cmd/drive/stale_mount_test.go, cmd/drive/stale_mount_e2e_test.go because they prove the files in scope. in-run review: unavailable - 124 ## What changed - The systemd unit runs a findmnt-gated `fusermount3 -uz` (then `fusermount`) as `ExecStartPre`, so a restart does not hit "directory already mounted" and does not unmount a non-FUSE filesystem (`cmd/drive/mount.go:535`). - The launchd item force-unmounts the folder only when `mount -t nfs` lists it (`cmd/drive/mount.go:475`). A plain umount is not tried first, because a hard NFS mount hangs it. - `drive mount` clears a stale entry before `MkdirAll` (`cmd/drive/mount.go:1151`). A live answering mount is left alone. An ENOTCONN create is `stale-mount`, not disk space (`cmd/drive/messages.go:178`). Other create failures still mention a full disk (`cmd/drive/messages.go:174`). - `Unmount` always calls `stopMount`, even when the login item is already gone (`cmd/drive/mount.go:1116`). `drive unmount` still runs that path when findmnt times out (`cmd/drive/main.go:395`) and then says what it did (`cmd/drive/main.go:409`). - `drive status` names a listed-but-dead mount, or a listing timeout, as stale. The next step is only `drive unmount` (`cmd/drive/status.go:163`). ## Verification: semgrep (diff-scoped, baseline origin/main): ``` SEMGREP_EXIT:0 ``` Acceptance: the unit and the launchd item run a cleanup step before start. ``` $ go test ./cmd/drive -count=1 -timeout 60s -v -run 'TestSystemdUnitClearsADeadFuseEntryBeforeStart|TestLaunchdPlistClearsADeadMountBeforeStart' === RUN TestSystemdUnitClearsADeadFuseEntryBeforeStart --- PASS: TestSystemdUnitClearsADeadFuseEntryBeforeStart (0.00s) === RUN TestLaunchdPlistClearsADeadMountBeforeStart --- PASS: TestLaunchdPlistClearsADeadMountBeforeStart (0.00s) ``` Acceptance: `drive unmount` on a stale findmnt entry leaves no mount. Acceptance: `drive unmount` still runs when findmnt times out. ``` === RUN TestUnmountClearsAStaleFindmntEntry --- PASS: TestUnmountClearsAStaleFindmntEntry (0.02s) === RUN TestRunUnmountClearsAHungFindmntEntry drive: unmounted /tmp/TestRunUnmountClearsAHungFindmntEntry234258618/001/Drive --- PASS: TestRunUnmountClearsAHungFindmntEntry (4.01s) ``` Acceptance: `drive status` names the stale mount and the one command that clears it. Acceptance: an ENOTCONN create is `stale-mount`, not disk space. Acceptance: a live answering mount is not lazy-unmounted. ``` === RUN TestMountViewTreatsAListingFailureAsStale --- PASS: TestMountViewTreatsAListingFailureAsStale (0.00s) === RUN TestRenderMountState --- PASS: TestRenderMountState (0.00s) === RUN TestDriveFolderMessageDoesNotBlameDiskSpace --- PASS: TestDriveFolderMessageDoesNotBlameDiskSpace (0.00s) === RUN TestClearStaleMountDirLeavesALiveFindmntEntry --- PASS: TestClearStaleMountDirLeavesALiveFindmntEntry (0.00s) === RUN TestClearStaleMountDirTreatsAHungListingAsStale --- PASS: TestClearStaleMountDirTreatsAHungListingAsStale (2.00s) ``` Acceptance: kill -9 on a live stand-in mount, then `drive mount` succeeds and the queued save uploads. Ran inside `unshare -Urm` because this host's default namespace cannot FUSE-mount. ``` $ unshare -Urm -- env CI=true go test ./cmd/drive -count=1 -timeout 180s -v -run TestStandinMountProofKillNineRecoversQueuedSave === RUN TestStandinMountProofKillNineRecoversQueuedSave --- PASS: TestStandinMountProofKillNineRecoversQueuedSave (6.70s) PASS ok github.com/Nishfleet/drive/cmd/drive 6.716s ``` Acceptance: go test is green (CI shape: race + short). PRE-EXISTING on this host: `TestLogoutStopsALiveMount` fails on origin/main `4bc72c3` under CI=true with `a FUSE skip is a failure under CI=true (drive#501)`. The same test was skipped here. ``` $ go test -race ./cmd/drive/ -short -count=1 -timeout 180s -skip TestLogoutStopsALiveMount ok github.com/Nishfleet/drive/cmd/drive 82.656s ``` ``` $ go vet ./cmd/drive/ VET:0 ``` Closes #542 --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is disabled.
